claim: Of the 103 passages in the pur- corpus at the stanza unit, 21 state a count of the fort word and 82 state none.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, 49 numeral rows over 30 passages: 27 adjudicated COUNTS-PUR over 21 distinct stanzas, 2 COUNTS-SERIES-COMPLETION, 20 COUNTS-OTHER; built by 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-counts.py and rv-pur-counts-adjudicate.py
notes: Denominator 103 = the etymological pur- family at the stanza unit (106 tokens, 104 padas, 103 stanzas, 86 hymns). 82 of 103 is 79.6 percent of the corpus carrying NO count. Any statement of the form 'the Rigveda says there were N forts' is drawn from a fifth of the passages that mention forts at all.

claim: Among the 21 passages stating a cardinal count of forts, 100 is stated in 9, ninety-nine in 6, seven in 4 and ninety in 2; two of the ninety-nine passages add an ordinal 'the hundredth' which modifies a dwelling word rather than the fort word.
notes: Counts sum to 21 distinct passages; the two ordinal passages are inside the 99 set and are not counted twice. CORRECTED: RV 6.31.4 was first read as 'hundreds' (satani, plural) and given its own category. That was wrong — satani there is the same form as sata at RV 1.53.8, ACC.N.PL, which this register reads as 'a hundred', and Griffith, Geldner and Grassmann are unanimous for 'a hundred' at 6.31.4. The 'other counts' heading of constitution section 4J therefore resolves to SEVEN alone, not to seven plus an unbounded plural.

claim: Ninety-nine is NOT the modal count of forts in the Rigveda. One hundred is, by 9 passages to 6.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv as PUR4J-002. 9 passages state 100 and 6 state 99.
notes: This answers the question 06-BRIEFS/rv01-reconciliation.md left open at section 2.6 item 2 ('whether 99 is the modal count, the maximal count, or merely the most quotable'). It is neither modal nor maximal: 100 is more frequent and 1000 is larger. It is the most quotable. CORRECTED from '8 to 6' when RV 6.31.4 was re-read as 100 rather than as 'hundreds'; the direction of the finding was unaffected and the margin widened.

claim: Ninety-nine is never expressed by a single numeral. In all six passages it is two words, nava 'nine' and navati- 'ninety', joined by ca in three of them and separated by other words in four.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, expression column. RV 1.54.6d puro navatim dambhayo nava; 2.19.6c navatim ca nava; 4.26.3b nava sakam navatih; 7.19.5b nava yat puro navatim ca; 7.99.5b nava puro navatim ca; 8.93.2a nava yo navatim puro
notes: The reconciliation brief section 2.6 item 1 flagged that 'even 99 is attested is a claim about a reading'. Tested here and upheld: the reading is secure, because all three full-coverage translators independent of one another on this point (Griffith, Geldner, Grassmann) render 99 at all six, and the padapatha analyses the words separately. But the object is a two-word expression, not a numeral.

claim: navati- 'ninety' is a feminine SINGULAR collective governing a plural puras in five of the six ninety-nine passages; only at RV 4.26.3 does it appear as an agreeing plural navatih.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, numeral_morph column: case=ACC|gender=F|number=SG at RV 1.54.6, 2.19.6, 7.19.5, 7.99.5, 8.93.2 and at the two ninety passages 1.130.7 and 3.12.6; case=ACC|gender=F|number=PL at RV 4.26.3
notes: Consequence for method, not only for grammar: a numeral-noun AGREEMENT test scored on case, gender and number under-reports navati- by construction, returning PARTIAL for a numeral that governs its noun perfectly well. Six rows of the counts register record this override explicitly. A mechanical agreement test run without this correction would drop five of the six ninety-nine passages.

claim: The identical nava-plus-navati- expression counts RIVERS, not forts, at RV 10.104.8, in a stanza that also carries the fort-word epithet purbhid.
locator: RV 10.104.8c navatim srotya nava ca sravantir; padapatha navatim | srotyah | nava | ca | sravantih. claim: Sambara's forts are counted at ninety-nine in three passages and at one hundred in two, with an ordinal 'hundredth' completing the ninety-nine at RV 4.26.3.
locator: RV 2.19.6 ninety-nine (sambarasya, genitive); RV 4.26.3 ninety-nine (sambarasya) plus satatamam vesyam in pada c; RV 7.99.5 ninety-nine (sambarasya); RV 2.14.6 one hundred (satam sambarasya puro); RV 6.31.4 one hundred (satani ... sambarasya puro).
notes: SUPERSEDES this row's first wording, which claimed that ninety, ninety-nine, one hundred, 'the hundredth' and 'hundreds' all attach to Sambara across six passages — that every count value section 4J enumerates attaches to this one opponent. Three of those five were wrong. (1) RV 1.130.7 does NOT count Sambara's forts: 'bhinat puro navatim indra purave / divodasaya' breaks the ninety FOR Puru and Divodasa, datives, while Sambara stands in a separate clause as what is hurled from the mountain, with no genitive attaching the forts to him. The first version rested on Sambara merely occurring in the stanza — the exact inference PUR4J-006 and rigveda-pur-counts.csv row PUR-N-038 declare invalid. (2) 'The hundredth' was withdrawn as a fort count by this unit's own COUNTS-SERIES-COMPLETION verdict and this row was not updated with it; it is retained here only as the completion of the ninety-nine at 4.26.3, which is what PUR4J-008 says it is. (3) 'Hundreds' at RV 6.31.4 is one hundred (PUR4J-002). What survives is five passages and two values, and those two values are the pair PUR4J-008 argues are one schema. Demoted to PROVISIONAL: the row is a reading of which forts belong to whom, not a count, and method note section 7 holds that VERIFIED rows are counts, forms, glosses or printed renderings. All three errors ran in the same direction, toward the deflationary conclusion; that is recorded in BF-014.

claim: In two of the six ninety-nine passages the ninety-nine is immediately followed by an ordinal 'the hundredth', applied to a dwelling word rather than to the fort word.
locator: RV 4.26.3: pada a-b nava sakam navatih ... purah, pada c satatamam vesyam 'the hundredth dwelling/inhabitant'. RV 7.19.5: pada b nava yat puro navatim ca, pada c nivesane satatama 'the hundredth in the settlement'.
notes: The ninety-nine and the hundredth are one schema: ninety-nine plus one completes a hundred. Note that satatama- does not modify pur- in either passage, so a search for numerals attached to the fort word alone would miss the completion that gives the ninety-nine its shape.

claim: Exactly three lemmas describe the material of a pur- in the Rigveda: ayasa- 'of metal' in 8 passages, asmanmaya- 'of stone' in 1, and ama- 'raw, unbaked' in 1. Ten of 103 passages state a material at all.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-fields.csv, material column. ayasa-: RV 1.58.8, 2.20.8, 4.27.1, 7.3.7, 7.15.14, 7.95.1, 8.100.8, 10.101.8. asmanmaya-: RV 4.30.20. ama-: RV 2.35.6. Descriptors identified by full case-gender-number agreement with a pur- family token; 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-fields.py

claim: Only one of the eight metal forts, RV 2.20.8, is the stronghold of a named adversary that is stormed. The other seven are protective, confining-in-a-myth, predicative, or an instruction to priests; in two of them the fort IS a god or a river.
locator: RV 1.58.8 Agni asked to protect the singer WITH iron forts; 2.20.8 Indra casts down the Dasyus' iron forts (the only enemy fort); 4.27.1 a hundred iron forts CONFINE the speaking eagle; 7.3.7 Agni asked to protect us with a hundred iron forts; 7.15.14 'pur bhava satabhujih' — Agni asked to BE an iron pur; 7.95.1 'sarasvati dharunam ayasi puh' — the river Sarasvati IS an iron pur; 8.100.8 the falcon escapes the iron fort; 10.101.8 'purah krnudhvam ayasir adhrsta' — priests told to MAKE iron forts.
notes: The measurement that bears hardest on constitution section 4J's instruction not to translate pur automatically into a Mature Harappan city. The metal forts are overwhelmingly not enemy settlements, and in two passages the fort is a god or a river. A reading that takes ayasa- pur- as evidence of metal-using fortified settlements has to account for the seven, not only the one. One reading is anticipated here rather than left for a reviewer. RV 4.27.1 and 8.100.8, where a hundred metal forts confine the eagle in the Soma-theft myth, could be called hostile: something adversarial is holding the bird. They are counted among the seven because the claim is about a specific thing — the stronghold of a NAMED adversary, stormed — and in those two the holder is unnamed, the setting is a myth of Soma's descent rather than a raid, and the action is escape rather than assault. Counting them as hostile instead would make it 3 of 8 rather than 1 of 8, and would not disturb the finding the claim supports: on either count a majority of the metal forts are not enemy settlements, and RV 7.15.14 and 7.95.1, where the fort is Agni and the river Sarasvati, are unaffected either way. Demoted from VERIFIED to PROVISIONAL on review: this row is a hand classification or a reading, and 04-AUDITS/rigveda-pur-4j-method.md section 7 holds that every VERIFIED row is a count, a form, a gloss or a printed rendering. PUR4J-025 to PUR4J-027, which are the same kind of judgement, were already PROVISIONAL; these were not, and the inconsistency was the reviewer's finding.

claim: The corpus names exactly one fort. RV 1.149.3 has puram narminim, and Grassmann glosses narmin- as 'Name (oder Beiwort) einer pur-' — name or epithet of a pur.
locator: RV 1.149.3a 'a yah puram narminim adided'. Geldner: 'Der die Burg Narmini beschien'. Griffith: 'He who hath lighted up the joyous castle'.
notes: Griffith reads narmini- as an adjective ('joyous') and Geldner as a proper name ('the fort Narmini'). Grassmann's own gloss declines to choose. So the claim that the Rigveda names a fort rests on one word whose word-class is disputed by the two translators, and the register records the dispute rather than resolving it. If Geldner is right this is the only named fort in 103 passages; if Griffith is right there are none.

claim: Geldner's per-hymn group heading names a poet for 55 of the 103 passages. For the other 48 it names a deity (45), a metre (1), a collection (1), or a strophe-type that is also a poet's name (1).
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-fields.csv, poet_lineage and poet_lineage_basis. 33 distinct headings; the largest are '2. group: hymns to Indra' (26 passages) and '1. group: hymns to Agni' (11), both of which name a deity.
notes: The 48 are typed NOT PRODUCED, not anonymous: Geldner's headings are an arrangement, and where he arranged by deity he recorded no poet. The 55 that do carry a name carry it at three removes from composition — Geldner 1951 follows the Anukramani tradition, which post-dates the text. HOLD-006 records that no source independent of Geldner was reachable: GRETIL, archive.org and TITUS all returned 403 at the proxy (SRC-080 to SRC-083), having each returned 200 earlier the same day. The one genuinely ambiguous heading is '6. group: the Pragatha group' at RV 9.107.10: Pragatha is both a strophe-type and a poet's name and the heading does not say which it means. Counted as NOT a poet attribution, the conservative reading; reclassifying it would make the split 56/47.

claim: Of the 103 passages: 17 carry a water lemma, 13 a cattle lemma, 12 a treasure lemma, 7 a mountain lemma, and 6 carry sindhu-, the only lemma in the corpus that can name a river.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-fields.csv. Water led by ap- (8) and sindhu- (6); cattle by gav- ~ go- (5) and vraja- (3); treasure by dhana- (2) and rayi- ~ ray- (2); mountain by adri- (3) and giri- (2). An independent scan of all 721 lemmas for a Grassmann gloss marking a river name returns sindhu- and nothing else; a scan for a mountain NAME returns nothing at all.
notes: Presence of a lemma in a passage, not a claim that the fort had water, cattle or treasure in it. Each field was DEFINED before it was filled, by a rule over Grassmann's glosses for all 721 lemmas occurring in the passages. Two exclusions were needed and both changed the result: bahuvrihi 'having X' epithets (without which treasure returns 56 lemmas, mostly epithets of Indra) and owner words (without which pati- 'Herr, Gebieter, Besitzer' enters treasure in 5 passages on the string Besitz). The river column is headed river_lemma_present, not 'named river': see PUR4J-028. No lemma in the 103 passages is glossed as the name of a mountain, so section 4J's 'mountain or river' resolves to common nouns for high ground plus one ambiguous hydronym.

claim: pur- is a feminine root noun. 67.5 percent of its 83 simplex tokens are accusative and 3.6 percent are locative: three tokens of 83.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-family-occurrences.csv, morphology column. ACC.PL puraḥ 45, ACC.SG puram 11 (56 of 83); LOC.SG puri 2, LOC.PL pursu 1 (RV 2.35.6c amasu pursu). Also GEN.PL puram 10, INS.PL purbhiḥ 6, NOM.SG puḥ 5, NOM.PL puraḥ 2, INS.SG pura 1.
notes: A measurement of case distribution, not an interpretation of it. Recorded because it is the single most awkward figure for any reading that makes pur- a settlement: the commonest thing a pur does in the Rigveda is be the direct object of a verb, and it is almost never a place anyone is said to be in.

claim: Griffith renders ayasa- as 'iron' in all eight of its passages; Geldner renders it 'ehern' (of ore, brass, bronze) in all eight. The two translators are systematically describing different metals, and neither argues the point.
locator: RV 1.58.8, 2.20.8, 4.27.1, 7.3.7, 7.15.14, 7.95.1, 8.100.8, 10.101.8. Griffith 'iron' 8/8. Geldner 'ehern' 8/8. Grassmann mixes: Erz at 1.58.8, Eisen at 4.27.1, ehern at the rest, and does not render the word at 7.3.7.
notes: Recorded as an OPEN CRUX with a named consequence, not as a finding either way. The two metals have different histories in South Asia, so which is meant bears on when the passages could have been composed, and a translator's single lexical habit can therefore move a chronology. No source retrieved in this unit settles it and nothing here asserts either reading. This is what constitution section 7 means by not letting the translation decide the historical question.

locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-typology.csv, columns inferred_geography, archaeological_fortification, unsupported_identification, all reading NOT ASSIGNED on all 103 rows, with why_three_types_unassigned on every row. Reasoning in 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-typology.py docstring.

claim: On the two text-decidable types, the 103 passages classify as 49 textual stronghold, 46 poetic formula, 3 both, and 5 that cannot be classified from the text.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-typology.csv. Poetic sub-kinds: DIVINE-EPITHET 28, SIMILE 8, METAPHOR 5, PROTECTIVE-FORMULA 5. Nine rule outputs overridden by hand, each with its reason on the row.
notes: PROVISIONAL, not VERIFIED: the rules are reproducible but the assignment is a reading. TEXTUAL-STRONGHOLD means the TEXT presents a fort as an object in its own narrative world; it is NOT a claim that any fort existed, was fortified or can be located. The five unclassifiable passages are RV 1.149.3 (narminim: proper name or adjective, Geldner against Griffith), 2.35.6 (a locative but the subject is Apam Napat), 5.66.4 (three translators give three different things), 8.1.28 (Susna's MOVING fort, a descriptor that rules out the ordinary sense without supplying a replacement) and 10.138.4 (a pur implied by a derived adjective and never named). These figures are the corrected ones. A stress test of rule R5 — asking which TEXTUAL-STRONGHOLD passages have neither a breaking root nor a named opponent — exposed a systematic gap: the corpus builds the puramdara- epithet ANALYTICALLY too, with a genitive plural puram depending on an agent noun of breaking (puram bhindur, puram dartar-, puram darman-), and those tokens are simplex pur- so rule R1 could not see them. Nine of the ten genitive-plural passages are this; the tenth, RV 4.30.20, is a genuine object where puram is governed by satam. Two metaphors (RV 7.52.1, 8.80.7) and one iva-simile (RV 6.2.7) were missed for related reasons. Before the correction the split was 60/35; after it, 49/46.

claim: All six passages stating ninety-nine forts are textual strongholds. The formulaic character of the COUNT does not make the PASSAGES formulaic.
locator: Cross-tabulation of 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-typology.csv against rigveda-pur-counts.csv. 99: 6 of 6 TEXTUAL-STRONGHOLD. 90: 2 of 2. Seven: 4 of 4. One hundred: 4 TEXTUAL-STRONGHOLD, 3 POETIC-FORMULA, 1 BOTH — the poetic ones are the protective 'guard us with a hundred forts' passages. Of the 21 counting passages, 17 are textual strongholds.
notes: The load-bearing distinction of this unit, and the reason the counts and the typology are separate registers. PUR4J-I-01 finds the ninety-nine a formulaic quantity; this row records that the six passages carrying it nevertheless present forts as objects that are held and broken. 'The number is a formula' and 'the passage is a formula' are different claims and the evidence separates them.

claim: Eight of the ten passages stating a material are NOT plain textual strongholds: four are poetic formulas, three are both, one cannot be classified.
locator: Cross-tabulation as PUR4J-026. Of the 10 material passages: POETIC-FORMULA 4 (metaphor at RV 7.15.14 and 7.95.1, protective formula at RV 1.58.8 and 7.3.7), BOTH 3 (RV 4.27.1, 8.100.8, 10.101.8), TEXTUAL-STRONGHOLD 2 (RV 2.20.8, 4.30.20), CANNOT-CLASSIFY 1 (RV 2.35.6).

The passages that say what a fort was made of are overwhelmingly the passages where the fort is a figure, a god, a river or a myth. The two exceptions are the only two enemy forts with a stated material: RV 2.20.8 (metal, the Dasyus') and RV 4.30.20 (stone, for Divodasa). Anyone reading fort materials as evidence for building technique is reading mostly figurative passages.

claim: sindhu- is the only lemma in the 103 passages that can name a river, and it is ambiguous between the common noun and the proper name. Griffith and Geldner read it differently across the six passages.
locator: Grassmann's gloss: 'Fluss, Strom; der Indus'. RV 1.103.8 and 1.109.8, sindhuḥ NOM.SG.F in a refrain listing Mitra, Varuna, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth and Heaven — a proper name for both translators. RV 10.111.10 sindhum ACC.SG.M — 'to Sindhu' Griffith, 'zum Sindhu' Geldner, proper for both. RV 10.104.8 sindhum ACC.SG.M — 'the ocean' Griffith against 'die Sindhu' Geldner, DISPUTED. RV 7.95.1 sindhur — 'the flood' Griffith, 'der Strom' Geldner, common noun for both. RV 10.89.7 sindhun ACC.PL.M — 'the rivers', common noun and plural.
notes: Corrects this unit's own earlier wording, which said a named river occurs in six passages and was the Sindhu in all six. Two of the six are common nouns for both translators, one is disputed between them, and three are proper names. The register column was renamed river_lemma_present accordingly and carries the caveat on every row. This matters because a hydronym is the only thread in the corpus that could ever reach a geography, and the thread is thinner than a lemma count makes it look.

claim: Correcting the typology's largest error moved 11 of 103 passages and changed none of the unit's headline findings.
locator: Before the periphrastic-epithet correction: 60 TEXTUAL-STRONGHOLD, 35 POETIC-FORMULA. After: 49 and 46. claim: 22 of 103 passages carry a patron-side name and 22 an opponent-side name, on Grassmann's classification of the name.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-fields.csv, patron_candidates and opponent_candidates. Opponent side led by sambara- (9 passages), pipru- (6), susna- (6); patron side by puru- (6), rjisvan- (5), purukutsa- (3).
notes: The columns carry Grassmann's classification of the NAME, not a reading of any passage's syntax, and every row says so; a name can occur in a passage without holding or attacking anything in it. The first run of the sort was WRONG in a way worth recording: purukutsa- and trasadasyu- were placed on the opponent side because the string 'Dasyu' matches inside TRASAdasyu and inside Purukutsa's own gloss 'des Trasadasyu Vater'. Both are glossed Schutzling, protege, and Purukutsa is the patron of the seven-fort cycle (PUR4J-010), so the bug put the register in contradiction with this unit's own claim. Fixed with word boundaries, with an explicit protege marker that settles the side when a gloss names both, and with a deity filter that keeps varuna- out of the patron column on the string Gotterkonig. Opponent candidates fell from 26 passages to 22.

claim: The numeral scan reaches 26 candidate lemmas over the 103 passages. It covers the 585 of 721 lemmas that carry a Grassmann gloss; the stem fallback for the other 136 returns nothing.
locator: 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-numeral-scan.py, which prints its own coverage: 11 candidates from an unambiguous number word, 15 from an ambiguous one, 0 from the stem fallback. Adjudication in 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-counts.py NUMERALS and EXCLUDED.
notes: SUPERSEDES this unit's earlier statement that the numeral inventory came from 'an exhaustive scan of the corpus's own lexicon' returning 12 candidates. That scan was not exhaustive and leaked three ways: it reached only glossed lemmas (81 percent of the lexicon); its word boundaries made hundert fail on the compound hundertfache; and it read no Latin, so satabhuji- glossed 'centuplex' was invisible. Four numeral-bearing lemmas were missed — satabhuji-, satamagha-, satatman-, prathama- — all now adjudicated with reasons. None is a count of forts, so no count in PUR4J-002 changes; but the exhaustiveness claim was false and the script that produced the figure was not committed, so the number could not be checked. Both are repaired. The stem fallback returning zero is now a DEMONSTRATION that the 136 glossless lemmas cost nothing here, where before it was an assumption.

claim: satabhuji- 'hundredfold' agrees in full with the fort word at RV 7.15.14 and RV 1.166.8 and is NOT counted as a fort count.
locator: RV 7.15.14c 'pur bhava satabhujih', satabhujih NOM.F.SG against puh NOM.F.SG. RV 1.166.8a 'satabhujibhis ... purbhih', INS.F.PL against INS.F.PL. Griffith 'with hundred walls' and 'With castles hundredfold'; Geldner 'mit hundert Ringen' and 'Mit hundertfachen Burgen'.
notes: Besides navatih at RV 4.26.3 these are the only full case-gender-number agreements between a numeral-bearing word and the fort word in the corpus, which is why the exclusion needs arguing rather than asserting. It is excluded because it does not say there are a hundred forts; it says ONE fort is hundredfold, and all four renderings by the two translators who reach these passages are adjectival. It is recorded instead as a DESCRIPTOR in rigveda-pur-fields.csv and in 06-BRIEFS/pur-translation-standard.md section 4. PROVISIONAL because the judgement is a reading and the opposite reading — 'with a hundred ramparts' shading into 'a hundred forts' at RV 1.166.8, where the noun is plural — is available. If it were counted, 100 would be stated in 11 passages rather than 9 and the margin over 99 would widen.
